Person Perception: Making Judgments About Others, Attribution Theory
When we observe people, we attempt to develop explanations of why they behave in certain ways.
Attribution theory-Proposed to develop explanations of the ways in which we judge people differently, depending on what meaning we attribute/assign to a given behaviour.
when we observe an individual’s behavior, we attempt to determine whether it was internally or externally caused.
The determination is based on 3 factors: Distinctiveness, consensus (common) & consistency.

slides.title: Factors influencing internal and external attributions
slides.text:
Factors influencing internal and external attributions
Distinctiveness - consistency of a person’s behavior across situations.
Coming late to work, blow off commitments.
Whether the behavior is unusual??
Unusual behavior- an external attribution
If it is not, it’ll probably be judged as internal.
Consensus – if everyone who faces a similar situation responds in the same way, the behavior shows consensus.
Employees who took the same route to work, were late.
High consensus- external attribution
Low consensus- internal attribution

slides.notes: The Johari window model is used to enhance the individual’s perception on others. This model is based on two ideas- trust can be acquired by revealing information about you to others and learning yourselves from their feedbacks. Each person is represented by the Johari model through four quadrants or window pane. Each four window panes signifies personal information, feelings, motivation and whether that information is known or unknown to oneself or others in four viewpoints.

slides.text:
Any aspect that you do not know about yourself, but others within the group have become aware of, is in your blind area. With the help of feedback from others you can become aware of some of your positive and negative traits as perceived by others and overcome some of the personal issues that may be inhibiting your personal or group dynamics within the team.
It is possible to increase your open area by asking for feedback from people.
When feedback is given honestly to you it can reduce the size of your blind area.
Maybe you interrupt people before they have finished making their point which can cause frustration.
Alternatively people may always want to talk to you because you are a good listener.
Sometimes you don’t realize these aspects of your character until it is pointed out.
By working with others it is possible for you to discover aspects that neither of you may never have appreciated before.

slides.title: Attitude
slides.text:
Attitude
Allport (1935) defined an attitude as a mental or neural state of readiness, organized through experience, exerting a directive or dynamic influence on the individual’s response to all objects and situations to which it is related.
A simpler definition of attitude is a mindset or a tendency to act in a particular way due to both an individual’s experience and temperament.

slides.title: Components of Attitudes
slides.text:
Components of Attitudes
An attitude includes three components: an affect (a feeling & emotions), cognition (a thought or belief, knowledge), and behavior (an action, behavioral expectations predisposition to action, intentions ).
Cognitive component The opinion or belief segment of an attitude. Eg., “discrimination is wrong”
Affective Component The emotional or feeling segment of an attitude. Eg., “I don’t like Katson because she discriminates against minorities”.
Behavioral Component An intention to behave in a certain way toward someone or something. Eg., “I might choose to avoid Jass because of my feelings about him”.

slides.title: Changing Attitudes
slides.text:
Changing Attitudes
Attitude transformation takes time, effort, and determination, but it can be done.
Managers need to understand that attitude change takes time and should not set unrealistic expectations for rapid change (Moore, 2003).
Attitudes are formed and beliefs during childhood years, influenced not only by family, religion, and culture but also by socioeconomic factors. This socialization process affects a person’s attitude toward work and his or her related behavior over a lifetime through an individual’s socialization process. An individual’s socialization process includes his or her formation of values
To change a person’s attitude we need to address the cognitive and emotional components.
Providing new information is one method for changing a person’s attitude and therefore his or her behavior.

slides.title: An Example
slides.text:
An Example
A corporate manager Geeta- believes strongly that no company should pollute air or water.
Unfortunately, Geeta, because of the requirements of her job, is placed in a position of having to make decisions against her attitudes on pollution.
She knows that dumping the company’s sewage into the local river (which we shall assume is legal) is in the best economic interest of her firm.
What will she do?
Clearly, Geeta is experiencing a high degree of cognitive dissonance.

slides.title: The Ethical Dilemma
slides.text:
The Ethical Dilemma
Because of the importance of elements in this example, we cannot expect Geeta to ignore the inconsistency.
Ethical Dilemma- There are several paths she can follow to deal with her dilemma.
She can change her behavior (stop polluting the river).
She can reduce dissonance by concluding that the dissonant behavior is not so important after all. (I have got to make a living, and in my role as a corporate decision maker, I often have to place the good of my company above that of the environment or society.)
Change her attitude- there is nothing wrong with polluting the river.
